[00:00] Sofia: Welcome everyone to the Redwood and Lumina Health conversation — um, thanks for joining, really excited to dive in. Quick intro, I'm Sofia Martinez, host — Ethan is running sound — and with me we have Dr. Maya Patel and Jordan Lee from Lumina. How are you folks?

[00:22] Sofia: Awesome. So, for listeners, a quick framing. Lumina Health uses Redwood Inference, uh, primarily in a private deployment for clinical summarization and automated patient messaging. Today we'll talk about why you picked Redwood, what changed operationally, and what results you're seeing. Maya, can you kick us off — what's the one-line use case?
[00:42] Maya: Yeah sure. So, one line — we use Redwood to power our discharge summaries and patient outreach, um, so clinicians get concise notes and patients get tailored follow-ups. Before Redwood we were stitching together a bunch of cloud endpoints and had latency issues plus PHI concerns.
[00:58] Sofia: Got it. Jordan, from a product/marketing lens, what was the business trigger?
[01:05] Jordan: We needed consistent quality and something that would scale — plus the security posture was non-negotiable. We had a pilot with an off-the-shelf API and the outputs were okay but inconsistent. Also cost was climbing as volumes rose. So we evaluated self-hosted runtimes and Redwood because Redwood offered a private (VPC/on-prem) option with good latency and an ops console.
[01:28] Sofia: Nice. Can you share any numbers? Percent improvements, latency, cost? Even ballpark.
[01:33] Maya: Sure — ballpark — generating a discharge summary used to take 8-12s on the old stack, now we're mid 2s to 3s per summary on average after tuning the batching and prefix caching. Cost-wise, it's like 40–60% lower per 1k summaries versus our previous hosted provider, once we accounted for reserved capacity and batching. And error rates — we saw fewer hallucinations after switching to the curated model variants; that's maybe anecdotal but our clinicians reported higher trust.
[02:05] Sofia: Lovely. There's a bunch to unpack — technical folks always wanna hear about the private deployment. Maya, how did the onboarding go? Any surprises?
[02:13] Maya: It was surprisingly smooth. Redwood's team — AE and SE — helped with the initial calibration. We ran a short benchmark (there's a spreadsheet we shared) and Redwood's SE helped tune kernel selection and quantization profile. The one surprise was our network egress rules; we had to open up some internal ports for KV cache syncing — that took a day. But overall, the private control plane made audits easier for us.
[02:38] Jordan: I can add — from the rollout side, we did a canary across 3 clinics, did 2 weeks of parallel runs, and then full rollout. The rollout tooling — canary + automatic fallback — was really helpful because we could route back to the older endpoint if there was a regression.
[02:57] [Ethan (off-mic) fiddles with audio]
[03:02] Sofia: Love that. For listeners curious about compliance — did SOC2 / ISO or KMS come up?
[03:09] Maya: Yes. KMS integration was critical. We use customer-managed keys for PHI at rest, and Redwood's audit logs fed into our SIEM. For SOC2 controls, Redwood provided the attestation docs we needed; we had a short questionnaire during procurement.
[03:24] Sofia: Procurement — always fun. Speaking of procurement, Jordan earlier mentioned cost savings. Were there procurement hurdles for reserved capacity?
[03:32] Jordan: We had to align finance and infra — reserved capacity had a commit, so we modeled usage for the year and that helped. The math worked because of predictable throughput and the batching which reduced per-token cost. Legal also wanted data residency guarantees but we use a VPC region aligned to our compliance needs.
[03:51] Sofia: Great. Let's talk about the user experience — clinician trust is big. Any process changes post-Redwood?
[03:58] Maya: We actually introduced a quick 'verify-and-sign' step; clinicians get the Redwood summary pre-populated in the EHR draft and can accept/edit. The edit rate dropped, which told us the quality was acceptable. Also, some clinicians now use the model's 'patient-friendly' rewriting for after-visit instructions.
[04:18] Jordan: From a metric perspective, average clinician time spent on notes reduced by about 12–15% in our early clinics — it's small but meaningful for clinician satisfaction.

[04:35] Sofia: Nice. Any hiccups after go-live?
[04:39] Maya: One incident — there was a latency spike when a batch job overlapped with peak clinical hours; Redwood suggested adjusting autoscaling policies and tweaking the batching window. After the change, it flattened out.
[04:55] Sofia: Sounds pragmatic. Listeners often ask about vendor lock-in — did you feel locked in?
[05:00] Jordan: We considered that. The policy-based routing and model pinning meant we could keep a fallback on an external provider during the pilot. So we didn't feel locked; Redwood's export and model versioning made it straightforward to switch if needed.

[05:18] Sofia: Favorite anecdote — Jordan or Maya?
[05:21] Maya: There's a small story — a clinician told me she saved 20 minutes on a complicated discharge because the model pulled all relevant meds and allergies into a concise paragraph. She was thrilled — it's those moments that sold the product internally.
[05:36] Jordan: We also got a positive patient NPS bump for post-discharge clarity — nothing huge but trending up in the pilot cohort.

[05:47] Sofia: Switching gears — any mentions of competitors during selection?
[05:51] Maya: We evaluated OpenAI, Anthropic, and some cloud vendor managed endpoints. Performance and the private deployment were the differentiators.
[05:59] Sofia: Perfect. For the case study we'd like to include a short quote — Jordan, could you give us 1–2 lines now that we might use on the website? Something about the impact or partnership.

[06:25] [00:06:25 — brief pause while Jordan checks notes]
[06:35] Sofia: Okay, quick lightning round — what's one piece of advice for other healthcare startups considering inference platforms?
[06:41] Maya: Prioritize data governance and run a realistic throughput benchmark. Don't just focus on raw latency numbers; consider batching, cache, and ops complexity.
[06:52] Jordan: Also, get legal and finance early — reserved capacity saves money but you need alignment.

[07:00] Sofia: Nice. We'll wrap with technical detail for listeners — can you briefly explain how batching and KV cache reduced cost and latency in practice? Keep it high level.
[07:10] Maya: Sure — batching lets many small requests be processed together to make GPU utilization efficient, and the KV cache keeps recent context tokens in a fast-access store so repeated prompts don't re-run the full context. Together they reduce per-token compute and thus cost; and when tuned, latency remains within our SLO.
